title: Muddy Road
text:
Two Zen monks, Tanzan and Ekido, were once walking together along a road that heavy rain had turned to deep mud. The downpour was still coming down.

At a bend in the road they came upon a lovely young woman in a silk kimono and sash. She stood at the edge of a stretch of mud, unable to cross without ruining her clothes.

"Come on, girl," said Tanzan at once. He lifted her in his arms, carried her over the mud and set her down on the other side. Then the two monks walked on.

Ekido did not say a word for the rest of the day. That night, when they had reached a temple where they could lodge, he could no longer restrain himself. "We monks do not go near women," he burst out, "especially not young and lovely ones. It is dangerous. Why did you do that?"

"I left the girl there," said Tanzan. "Are you still carrying her?"
lesson: Grievances and judgments you keep turning over in your mind weigh more than the event itself. Help when help is needed, then put it down.
people: Tanzan, Ekido, a girl in a kimono
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919)
